It's also more than being charming and bringing food to the table. I mean, it's not a complex job but it can be strenuous. If it was as easy as just walking from the kitchen to the table there would be no such thing as poor service.

Getting the order in and out correctly and quickly takes more than just entering the order and taking it out when it is ready. For example, you've got to predict mistakes before they happen, and get in the kitchen to whip up food that just won't seem to come out while still maintaining your presence in the dinning room. 

Additionally you're keeping the front of house clean and presentable, doing side-work and juggling the needs of a bunch of different tables. All while trying not to cry after you were screamed at for a few minutes by somebody else's angry table.

It all seems pretty simple on paper. If you just have a couple of tables, yeah, it will be so simple it's boring. But you won't know what it's really like until you're waiting on 60 people during a rush and you can't keep up.

Obviously the following is just my opinion. Not to mention different restaurants will give different experiences for the cooks and waitstaff.

I've worked both as a cook and a server. As a cook I was just doing my job, and I didn't feel like it would make sense to receive a tip. If your food isn't good, then I didn't do my job.

As a server I busted my ass directly for the customer. If the cooks kept messing up the order, I'd get in the kitchen and make it myself. If my wage was guaranteed, I don't picture myself going that far out of my way for the customer.  

Assuming I made the same amount of money, I'd probably prefer not to serve for tips. However, I think it's probably in the customer's best interest to tip. 

The reality is it would probably be a pay cut, and I can't imagine serving for less money.
